article.title: When Efficiency Creates More Demand: The Rebound Effect in AI Computing
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Efficiency is usually treated as an obvious way to reduce resource use. If a model needs less electricity for each inference, it seems natural to expect total electricity consumption to fall. At the level of one task, that reasoning is correct. At the level of an entire market, however, the outcome can be different. Lower cost can make a service attractive for many more uses, causing total demand to rise. Economists often describe this family of responses as a rebound effect.

Consider a simplified example. An AI service initially uses one unit of computing for each request and receives one million requests per day. Engineers then improve the system so that each request needs only half a unit. If demand stays unchanged, computing use falls from one million units to 500,000. But the lower cost may allow the company to reduce prices, increase usage limits, add AI to free products, or automate tasks that were previously too expensive. If requests rise to three million per day, total computing use becomes 1.5 million units. The service is twice as efficient per request but uses more computing overall.

This does not mean efficiency is useless. The improvement still creates real value: more work can be performed with each unit of computing. The mistake is assuming that a unit-level efficiency gain translates mechanically into an equal system-level reduction in resource consumption. The final outcome depends on how strongly demand responds to the lower effective cost.

AI is particularly interesting because many potential uses are still constrained by price and latency. A company may currently use a large model only for high-value customer interactions. If inference becomes ten times cheaper, the same company might summarize every internal document, analyze every support conversation, generate personalized material for millions of users, or run agents continuously in the background. Activities that once seemed economically unreasonable can become normal.

There are several channels through which rebound can occur. The intensive margin means existing users consume more of a service. The extensive margin means new users or new applications enter the market. A third channel is quality: developers may spend efficiency gains on larger context windows, more reasoning steps, higher-resolution inputs, or multiple model calls rather than reducing total compute. In practice, these channels can operate together.

This distinction matters for corporate planning. A technology team may forecast infrastructure needs by taking today's workload and multiplying it by an expected efficiency improvement. That forecast can be badly wrong if cheaper inference unlocks new products or changes user behavior. Capacity planning therefore needs both a technical efficiency assumption and a demand response assumption. Management should ask not only, 'How much cheaper will one task become?' but also, 'What will we choose to do once it becomes cheaper?'

The same issue appears in energy and climate discussions. More efficient chips, models, cooling systems, and data centres can reduce the electricity required for a fixed amount of AI output. Yet total sector electricity demand depends on the amount of AI output society chooses to consume. Strong growth in models, users, agents, and automated workflows can offset part or all of the savings from efficiency. This is why forecasts of data-centre electricity use need assumptions about deployment as well as hardware performance.

The rebound effect is not necessarily a policy failure. Increased consumption can represent genuine economic benefit. If cheaper AI helps scientists analyze more experiments or small firms access capabilities they could not previously afford, higher computing use may accompany higher productivity and welfare. The relevant question is not whether demand grows, but whether the benefits justify the additional resources and whether infrastructure can expand sustainably.

For investors, another implication is that efficiency can expand markets instead of simply shrinking costs. A dramatic decline in inference cost may reduce revenue per unit of compute but increase the number of economically viable workloads. Suppliers positioned across chips, networking, power, cooling, and software may therefore experience demand that does not fall as quickly as unit efficiency statistics suggest. The distribution of value can still change, so this is not a guarantee of higher profits.

Managers should separate three metrics: compute per task, cost per task, and total compute consumed. The first two describe unit economics; the third describes system demand. They can move in opposite directions. A useful forecast can model several demand elasticities rather than assuming fixed usage. If efficiency improves by 50 percent, what happens if demand rises by 20 percent, 100 percent, or 300 percent? Such scenarios expose the sensitivity of infrastructure requirements.

The broader lesson is that technology changes behavior. Efficiency does not occur in a vacuum. By lowering the effective price of an activity, it can change which activities people consider worthwhile. In AI computing, this means engineers can successfully reduce the resources needed for one inference while the industry simultaneously builds more infrastructure. There is no contradiction. One describes efficiency at the unit level; the other describes demand at the system level. Understanding both is essential for realistic capacity, energy, and investment planning.
paragraphs.zh: 效率提升不一定讓總資源使用下降。若每次 inference 所需算力減半，但成本下降刺激請求量增加三倍，總算力仍會上升，這類現象可用 rebound effect 理解。AI 特別容易出現反彈，因為很多用途目前仍受價格與 latency 限制；推理變便宜後，企業可能把 AI 放進更多產品、分析所有對話、持續運行 agents，或把效率節省用在更長 context、更多 reasoning steps。這不代表效率沒有價值，而是 unit-level efficiency 不能直接等同 system-level resource reduction。容量規劃應同時假設技術效率與 demand response，並分開看 compute per task、cost per task、total compute。能源與投資分析也應如此：更高效率可以擴大市場，而不是單純縮小基礎設施需求。
paragraphs.ja: 効率改善が総資源消費の減少につながるとは限りません。1回のinferenceに必要なcomputeが半分になっても、低価格によってrequestが3倍になれば総computeは増えます。このような反応はrebound effectとして理解できます。AIでは価格やlatencyの制約で未実現の用途が多く、推論が安くなると、より多くの製品、全会話の分析、常時agent、長いcontext、追加reasoningなどへ利用が広がります。効率改善自体には価値がありますが、unit-level efficiencyをsystem-level resource reductionと同一視してはいけません。capacity planningでは技術効率とdemand responseの両方を仮定し、compute per task、cost per task、total computeを分けて見る必要があります。

vocabulary.usage: Efficiency can create a rebound in demand.
The intensive margin captures more use by existing users.
The extensive margin adds new users.
Higher use may increase economic welfare.
Price can be a constraint on adoption.

quiz.answer: Lower cost can increase usage enough to offset the unit-level savings.
